name: Erez-Rosen Quadrupole
description: Schwarzschild's metric with a mass quadrupole added, a static vacuum field of Weyl's class found by G. Erez and Nathan Rosen in 1959. For every quadrupole parameter $q \neq 0$ a naked curvature singularity stands where the horizon was, which Doroshkevich, Zel'dovich, and Novikov used in 1965 to argue that a collapsing star sheds its quadrupole.
convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ is a length and the quadrupole parameter $q$ is a pure number. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Stars and planets are not round: they spin and they bulge, and astrometry is now sharp enough that the quadrupole moment of Jupiter shows in the path of light that skims the planet [bini2013]. Karl Schwarzschild's solution of 1916 is the field of a perfect sphere, with one number in it, the mass [schwarzschild1916]. Which exact field belongs to a mass that has a quadrupole moment as well?¶Hermann Weyl had turned half of that question into a problem of Newton's gravity in 1917 [weyl1917]. For a static vacuum field with an axis of symmetry his reduction leaves two functions: a potential $\psi$ that solves Laplace's equation of flat space, and a second function $\gamma$ found from $\psi$ by an integral [weyl1917, lehmkuhl2019]. Any Newtonian potential with an axis can therefore be promoted to a solution of Einstein's equations, and the puzzle is which one to promote, because in Weyl's coordinates Schwarzschild's sphere is the potential of a rod of length $2m$ [bicak2000]. G. Erez and Nathan Rosen, at the Technion in Haifa, took the puzzle up in 1959 [erez1959]. Their abstract proposes a procedure "for calculating the metric tensor describing the gravitational field of a particle possessing a mass multipole moment", worked through for a quadrupole [erez1959].¶The trick is in the coordinates: Erez and Rosen used prolate spheroidal ones, $x$ and $y$, which Hernando Quevedo calls "specially adapted to describe the gravitational field of non-spherically symmetric bodies" [quevedo2012]. In them the rod's potential depends on $x$ alone, $\psi = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\frac{x - 1}{x + 1}$, and the solutions of Laplace's equation that die away at infinity come one to a multipole, with Schwarzschild's the first [quevedo2012]. Erez and Rosen added the quadrupole with a number $q$ in front, $$\psi = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{x - 1}{x + 1} + \frac{q}{2}\left(3y^2 - 1\right)\left[\frac{1}{4}\left(3x^2 - 1\right)\ln\frac{x - 1}{x + 1} + \frac{3}{2}x\right],$$ so that $q = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric again [quevedo2012, bini2013].¶Then came $\gamma$, an integral over squares of the derivatives of $\psi$ that runs to three lines of logarithms, and the printed answer was wrong [doroshkevich1965, young1969]. A. G. Doroshkevich, Yakov Zel'dovich, and Igor Novikov reprinted the solution in a paper submitted in December 1964, "after correction of the error that has crept into" the original, an error that "changes the final form of the formulas appreciably" [doroshkevich1965]. Jeffrey Winicour, Allen Janis, and Ezra Newman corrected the coefficients in 1968, and John Young and C. Alton Coulter stated the corrected metric once more in 1969, for what they called "this experimentally significant case" [winicour1968, young1969, boshkayev2019]. The English translation of Doroshkevich, Zel'dovich, and Novikov's paper carries a slip of its own: it prints $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + q + q^2)$ where Weyl's equations ask for $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + q)^2$ [doroshkevich1965, quevedo2012].¶Why did Zel'dovich's group want the formula? They were asking whether a star that collapses out of round leaves a lopsided field behind [doroshkevich1965]. In Erez and Rosen's field the surface where $g_{tt}$ vanishes, Schwarzschild's horizon at $q = 0$, is a true singularity for every other $q$: the curvature grows without bound there, and for a body "elongated along the axis like a cucumber" the equator of that surface shrinks to nothing while its meridians stretch to infinity [doroshkevich1965]. A star falling through its own Schwarzschild surface meets nothing of the kind, so they concluded that "the quadrupole and higher multipole moments of the external gravitational field attenuate during the relativistic stages of the collapse" [doroshkevich1965]. Werner Israel proved the general statement in 1967: among static vacuum fields with closed equipotential surfaces, Schwarzschild's is "the only one which has a nonsingular infinite-red-shift surface" [israel1967].¶The multipole moments that Robert Geroch and R. O. Hansen defined for curved space say what $q$ measures: the metric has mass $m$ and quadrupole moment $\tfrac{2}{15}qm^3$, prolate for positive $q$ and oblate for negative [geroch1970, hansen1974, boshkayev2019, bini2013]. By 1989 Quevedo had extended the construction to every multipole, and with Bahram Mashhoon he had set the mass spinning, in a metric that is Kerr's at $q = 0$ and Erez and Rosen's at rest [quevedo1989, quevedomashhoon1985, boshkayev2019]. Quevedo and Linda Parkes followed its geodesics the same year, and in 2013 Donato Bini and his coauthors traced its light rays with the Gaia mission in mind [quevedoparkes1989, bini2013]. The singularity at $r = 2m$ is still there, so Jan-Menno Memmen and Volker Perlick, who set tori of fluid circling the mass in 2021, take the metric as "valid only outside of a surface" that surrounds it, with an interior of matter matched on [memmen2021].

related.text: The round mass, $q = 0$. For every other $q$ the horizon at $r = 2m$ is a curvature singularity [doroshkevich1965].

The other deformation of Schwarzschild's metric by a quadrupole, which multiplies the rod's potential by a number $\delta$. There the deformation changes the mass, and here the mass is $m$ for every $q$ [memmen2021].

The exterior of a slowly rotating star, an approximate field with a quadrupole moment of its own. Without rotation and to first order in $q$ the two agree, once Zipoy and Voorhees's stretch $\delta = 1 + sq$ is applied to Erez and Rosen's metric [boshkayev2019].
The rotating black hole. Quevedo and Mashhoon's rotating deformed mass is Kerr's metric at $q = 0$ and Erez and Rosen's without rotation [boshkayev2019].
Another member of Weyl's class, built on the Newtonian potential of a point. Erez and Rosen's is built on the potential of Schwarzschild's rod with a quadrupole term added [bicak2000, boshkayev2019].

coordinates.name: Prolate Spheroidal

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass measured at spatial infinity
Quadrupole parameter, a pure number; the quadrupole moment is $\tfrac{2}{15}qm^3$ in units of length cubed, prolate for $q > 0$ and oblate for $q < 0$, and $q = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric
The logarithm of Schwarzschild's potential, which falls to $-\infty$ at $x = 1$ and rises to zero at infinity

Weyl's first function, Schwarzschild's $\tfrac{1}{2}L$ plus $q$ times the quadrupole harmonic that dies away at infinity; it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x\left(\left(x^2 - 1\right)\partial_x\psi\right) + \partial_y\left(\left(1 - y^2\right)\partial_y\psi\right) = 0$

Weyl's second function, fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_x\gamma = \dfrac{1 - y^2}{x^2 - y^2}\left(x\left(x^2 - 1\right)\left(\partial_x\psi\right)^2 - x\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(\partial_y\psi\right)^2 - 2y\left(x^2 - 1\right)\partial_x\psi\,\partial_y\psi\right)$ and $\partial_y\gamma = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 - y^2}\left(y\left(x^2 - 1\right)\left(\partial_x\psi\right)^2 - y\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(\partial_y\psi\right)^2 + 2x\left(1 - y^2\right)\partial_x\psi\,\partial_y\psi\right)$, and zero on the axis $y = \pm 1$

coordinates.convention: We use prolate spheroidal coordinates $(t, x, y, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$ and $y$ pure numbers, and write $L$ for $\ln\left((x - 1)/(x + 1)\right)$. Weyl's canonical coordinates are $\rho = m\sqrt{(x^2 - 1)(1 - y^2)}$ and $z = mxy$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass measured at spatial infinity
Quadrupole parameter, a pure number; the quadrupole moment is $\tfrac{2}{15}qm^3$ in units of length cubed, prolate for $q > 0$ and oblate for $q < 0$, and $q = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric
The logarithm of Schwarzschild's potential, which falls to $-\infty$ at $r = 2m$ and rises to zero at infinity

Weyl's first function, Schwarzschild's $\tfrac{1}{2}L$ plus $q$ times the quadrupole harmonic that dies away at infinity; it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_r\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\partial_r\psi\right) + \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta\left(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta\psi\right) = 0$

Weyl's second function, fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_r\gamma = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{r^2 - 2mr + m^2\sin^2\theta}\left(\left(r - m\right)\sin\theta\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\left(\partial_r\psi\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\theta\psi\right)^2\right) + 2\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\cos\theta\,\partial_r\psi\,\partial_\theta\psi\right)$ and $\partial_\theta\gamma = -\dfrac{\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\sin\theta}{r^2 - 2mr + m^2\sin^2\theta}\left(\cos\theta\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\left(\partial_r\psi\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\theta\psi\right)^2\right) - 2\left(r - m\right)\sin\theta\,\partial_r\psi\,\partial_\theta\psi\right)$, and zero on the axis $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ that are Schwarzschild's at $q = 0$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length, and write $L$ for $\ln\left(1 - 2m/r\right)$. The prolate spheroidal coordinates are $x = r/m - 1$ and $y = \cos\theta$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
